intent: I'm reading the AMS-02 solar-modulation modeling literature. When people model the proton-to-helium flux ratio (p/He) measured by AMS-02 and ask why it changes over time, especially below a few GV after the 2013 polarity reversal, what is identified as the dominant physical cause inside the transport model? I want the specific mechanism, not a hand-wave.
nuggets: The dominant cause of the time dependence of p/He below ~3 GV is the dependence of the diffusion tensor (diffusion coefficients) on the particle mass-to-charge ratio A/Z
A 3D steady-state numerical model solving Parker's transport equation is used to reproduce the AMS-02 monthly proton (and helium) fluxes between May 2011 and May 2017, rigidity 1-60 GV
Helium is assumed to have the same mean free paths / diffusion as protons, so the p/He time behavior is reproduced without separate diffusion for He
The A/Z dependence enters the diffusion coefficients through the particle speed beta (velocity term), which differs between p (A/Z=1) and He (A/Z~2) at the same rigidity
The model fits the monthly fluxes via a grid/ensemble of pre-computed models that is interpolated to minimize chi-squared, rather than a direct least-squares fit
rationale: Read Corti2018 full text (lines 22, 40, 142-144): abstract and body state explicitly 'The dependence of the diffusion tensor on the particle mass-to-charge ratio A/Z is found to be the main cause of the time dependence of p/He below 3 GV'; the 3D steady-state ADI Parker model and the grid-interpolation fit method are described in sections 2-3. Song2021 (line 28) and Ngobeni2020 (lines 9-11, 36) corroborate the A/Z + beta mechanism but are secondary discussions, hence context. This is a single-paper-anchored mechanism question; one paper truly answers it -> thin.

intent: I want to understand the standard methodology that the heliophysics community uses to reproduce the time variation of galactic cosmic-ray proton and helium spectra over a solar cycle with 3D numerical models. Specifically: what transport equation underlies these models, which transport parameter is found to carry most of the time variation as solar activity changes, and how does its behavior relate to solar activity? Synthesize across the modeling papers.
nuggets: The models numerically solve Parker's cosmic-ray transport equation, which includes the four processes of convection (outward solar wind), diffusion, gradient/curvature + current-sheet drift, and adiabatic energy changes

The magnitude/normalization of the (parallel) diffusion coefficient is the dominant parameter controlling modulation level and is anti-correlated with solar activity (larger diffusion / longer mean free path near solar minimum, smaller near maximum)

A single set of modulation parameters (same diffusion mean free paths) reproduces both proton and helium spectra simultaneously, i.e. the rigidity dependence of the mean free path is assumed the same for p and He
The models cover/span the 2006-2017 period including the solar magnetic field polarity reversal during the solar-maximum of cycle 24
Drift effects are charge/polarity dependent and get suppressed when diffusion becomes large (during the quiet solar minimum), contributing to the 22-year cycle
Solar-activity proxies fed into the models are the heliospheric current sheet tilt angle and the heliospheric magnetic field magnitude at Earth
rationale: All three gold papers explicitly: (Song2021 abstract+lines 184-193) 'K0 ... shows a clear time-dependent pattern ... the magnitude of the diffusion coefficients anticorrelated with solar activity' and reproduce p+He with one parameter set; (Corti2018 line 22,46) solves Parker eq with the 3D model; (Ngobeni2020 lines 9,42-51) 3D drift model reproduces PAMELA p and He 2006-2009 with same modulation params and lists convection/diffusion/drift/adiabatic. Wang2019 (2D model, also fits p/He/B/C and ties D to HMF) and Potgieter2021 (same model family, drift/22-yr) corroborate but are secondary framings -> context. Multi-paper synthesis with >=3 directly-answering papers in slice -> strong.

intent: What did the PAMELA satellite experiment actually find when it measured the cosmic-ray proton and helium spectra in rigidity, and why were those findings described as a challenge to the conventional picture of cosmic-ray acceleration in supernova remnants plus simple diffusive galactic propagation? I want the concrete spectral observations and the interpretation.
nuggets: PAMELA measured proton and helium spectra in the rigidity range ~1 GV to 1.2 TV (2006-2008 data)
Proton and helium have different spectral shapes / different spectral indices (the proton-to-helium flux ratio decreases smoothly with rigidity; proton index ~2.82, helium ~2.73, difference ~0.1)
Both spectra cannot be described by a single power law: the spectrum gradually softens around 30-230 GV and then shows an abrupt hardening at ~230-240 GV

These features (different p vs He slopes, and the breaks) challenge the standard paradigm of acceleration in supernova remnants followed by simple diffusive propagation, which predicts a single universal power law for all species
More complex / multiple-source acceleration and propagation processes are required to explain the observed spectral structures
rationale: Read Adriani2011 full text: abstract (line 30) and body lines 50-91 give the exact numbers - rigidity 1 GV-1.2 TV, gamma_p=2.820, gamma_He=2.732, Delta_gamma=0.101, softening 30-230 GV, hardening at 232/243 GV, single power law rejected at >=95% C.L., and lines 84-91 state it challenges the SNR+diffusive-propagation single-power-law paradigm (GALPROP fails). Single paper fully answers -> thin. Amato2017 (CR transport review) and MKachelriess2019 (CR models review) discuss these anomalies in general but are review context.

intent: I'm interested in using cosmic-ray antiprotons as a dark-matter probe. Using the precise AMS-02 antiproton data, what limits can be set on heavy (TeV-scale) dark matter annihilating into Standard Model final states, and is the thermal wino dark-matter scenario ruled in or out? Also how do these antiproton limits compare with gamma-ray limits from dwarf galaxies and the Galactic center?
nuggets: AMS-02 antiproton data are used to set 95% C.L. upper limits on the dark-matter annihilation cross section <sigma v> for all SM final-state channels, over DM masses ~200 GeV to 50 TeV

The analysis fits dark matter together with cosmic-ray propagation (GALPROP), using AMS-02 p, He and antiproton/proton data; secondary antiprotons alone fit the spectrum so no primary astrophysical antiproton component is required
The thermal wino (electroweak triplet) dark matter scenario is strongly disfavored / excluded by the antiproton limits, even with a conservative estimate of systematic uncertainties
For annihilation into quarks or gauge bosons the antiproton limits are significantly stronger than the gamma-ray limits from dwarf spheroidal galaxies
Cosmic-ray antiproton limits are more robust than Galactic-center gamma-ray/gamma-line limits, which depend sensitively on the (cuspy vs cored) DM density profile
rationale: Read Cuoco2017 full text: abstract (line 16) plus sections 2.1-2.4 (lines 30, 65-78, 105-119) give the mass range 200 GeV-50 TeV, all SM channels, the combined GALPROP fit, the result that the thermal wino is strongly disfavored even with conservative systematics, and the explicit comparison that antiproton limits beat dwarf-spheroidal limits for quark/gauge channels while being more robust than profile-dependent Galactic-center gamma-ray limits. Single paper answers fully -> thin. Potgieter2021 only motivates anti-nuclei as a DM test (context); not a quantitative DM-limit paper.

intent: What is the observational evidence from the Pierre Auger Observatory for anisotropy in the arrival directions of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, and which class of candidate sources gives the strongest correlation? I want the dataset size, the energy threshold, the significance, and the angular scale of the best-fitting model.
nuggets: The analysis uses 5514 Auger events above 20 EeV recorded before 30 April 2017, with zenith angles up to 80 degrees
A model based on starburst galaxies (SBGs, gamma-ray/radio-selected) fits the data better than isotropy with 4.0 sigma significance, with the maximum for events above 39 EeV
The best-fitting starburst model has an intermediate angular scale (search radius) of ~13 degrees and an anisotropic fraction of ~10% of events
A model based on gamma-ray active galactic nuclei (gamma-AGNs) is favored over isotropy at 2.7 sigma, best above 60 EeV, with a smaller ~7 degree angular scale
The anisotropy appears as an intermediate-scale excess (hotspot) of UHECRs, associated with the region around Centaurus A / nearby starburst galaxies

A maximum-likelihood ratio test against isotropy is used, with the two fit parameters being the anisotropic fraction and the angular search radius, and attenuation (GZK) of distant sources is accounted for
rationale: Read Aab2018 full text: abstract (line 9) and sections 2 & 4.2 (lines 33-37, 85-101 and the results table at 109-116) give 5514 events >20 EeV before 2017-04-30, starburst model 4.0 sigma above 39 EeV at 13 (+4/-3) degrees with 10+/-4% anisotropic fraction, gamma-AGN 2.7 sigma above 60 EeV at 7 degrees, the maximum-likelihood-ratio method, GZK attenuation handling, and the Centaurus A hotspot interpretation. Single paper answers fully -> thin. Batista2019 (UHECR open-questions review) and Mollerach2017 (high-energy CR review) mention anisotropy generally -> context.

intent: I'm reading up on the classical theory of solar modulation of cosmic rays and I keep seeing 'adiabatic deceleration' mentioned alongside convection. Can you explain physically what adiabatic deceleration of cosmic rays in the solar wind actually is, why it happens, and how large its effect is on the observed cosmic-ray spectrum compared with the outward convection by the solar wind?
nuggets: Adiabatic deceleration arises because, in the frame moving with the solar wind, cosmic rays random-walk through magnetic fields that are continually expanding (the radial wind has divergence nabla.v = 2v/r), so particles lose energy
Particles typically lose of order 5-20% of their original energy while penetrating into the solar system, and the energy loss slides the spectrum down the energy scale rather than removing particles
For a power-law interstellar spectrum the power-law form is preserved through the solar wind

Above ~10^9-10^10 eV (spectral index gamma ~2.5) adiabatic deceleration contributes about one third of the total depression of cosmic-ray density at a given energy, with outward convection contributing the other ~two thirds

At low energies (flat or rising spectrum, gamma < 1) the deceleration can instead produce an increase that partially cancels the convective reduction; over the whole spectrum deceleration produces zero net change in total particle density
rationale: Read Parker1966 full text (/data/paper-vault/extracts/md/Parker1966.md). The abstract and Sections 1, 3A, and 5 state verbatim: deceleration follows from random-walk through expanding fields (div.v = 2v/r), 5-20% energy loss, power-law preserved, ~one third of total modulation above 10^9-10^10 eV with convection ~two thirds, increase at low energies, and zero net density change. Every nugget is taken directly from this paper. Parker1958 (the original convection-diffusion paper) and the Engelbrecht2022 review touch the topic but the quantitative adiabatic-deceleration result is uniquely in Parker1966.

intent: I want a synthesis of Parker's cosmic-ray transport equation as it underpins modern solar-modulation modelling: which distinct physical processes does the equation describe, and how do recent heliospheric solar-modulation studies actually realize and numerically solve it? Pull together the original formulation and concrete modern applications that build on it.
nuggets: Parker's transport equation describes four physical processes acting on the cosmic-ray distribution: outward convection by the solar wind, diffusion (via the diffusion tensor K from magnetic-field fluctuations), adiabatic energy changes (cooling) in the expanding solar wind, and gradient/curvature/current-sheet drifts

The foundational pieces are Parker 1958 (solar wind sweeps/convects cosmic rays out of the inner solar system, depressing intensity) and Parker 1965/1966 (the transport equation including adiabatic deceleration)

A common modern solution method recasts the Fokker-Planck/Parker equation as an equivalent set of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) integrated as pseudo-particle trajectories, often in a time-backward formulation

Modern modulation work solves Parker's equation in 3D and time-dependently, fitting diffusion and drift coefficients to data (e.g. Song et al. 2021-based models used for AMS-02/PAMELA reproduction and astronaut dose, and the Potgieter/Vos 3D model used for HEPD-01/CSES-01 GCR proton spectra)

Drifts (entering via the antisymmetric part of the diffusion tensor) are responsible for charge-sign dependence and the 22-year modulation cycle, while adiabatic losses dominate the low-energy (below ~500 MeV) spectrum
rationale: Verified by reading: Engelbrecht2022 Eq.(1) and surrounding text spell out the four terms (convection, diffusion, adiabatic, drift) and the SDE history; Dunzlaff2015 Eq.(1) writes Parker's equation with the same labelled terms and develops the time-backward SDE pseudo-particle method; Parker1958 (full text) gives the convection-diffusion depression; Parker1966 gives adiabatic deceleration. Chen2023 confirms 'A new 3D and time-dependent solar modulation model based on Parker's transport equation' plus backward-time SDE/Wiener noise and per-Bartel-rotation diffusion/drift fitting to AMS-02/PAMELA; Martucci2023 confirms its 3D TPE (Parker 1965) with the four processes (convection, diffusion, adiabatic, drift) used to reproduce HEPD-01 proton spectra. All six are within slice [20:40] and each genuinely contributes. (Note: Chen2023/Martucci2023 were originally grep-verified rather than read in full when authored; both have SINCE been content-confirmed against full text — the grep-only caveat is lifted, drill 2026-06-02d.)

intent: For numerically solving Parker's transport equation for charged-particle transport in the heliosphere, why would someone use stochastic differential equations instead of finite-difference schemes, and what does running them on a GPU buy you? Explain the time-backward pseudo-particle approach and any concrete performance numbers.
nuggets: Parker's transport equation is recast into an equivalent set of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) solved by integrating many pseudo-particle trajectories (Euler-Maruyama scheme, first-order accurate in the time step) and averaging

SDEs are unconditionally stable, unlike finite-difference schemes that can go unstable for too-large time steps, and they avoid a spatial grid / matrix inversions (e.g. those needed by ADI finite-difference solvers)

The time-backward formulation releases pseudo-particles from the observation point and propagates them to the heliopause boundary, which is far more efficient than time-forward (where most particles released at the boundary never reach the observation point and are wasted) when intensities are needed at only a few phase-space points
Because pseudo-particle trajectories are independent, the problem is embarrassingly parallel and maps well to GPUs (one thread per pseudo-particle), implemented with CUDA

Measured GPU-vs-CPU (OpenMP, 8 threads) speedups are roughly a factor of ~12 for one partition and ~32 for 720 partitions without fast-math, rising to ~26 and ~59 with fast-math; an order-of-magnitude (10-60x) overall improvement

A transition-probability solution is independent of the boundary function, so fluxes/spectra for different boundary conditions (e.g. a different local interstellar spectrum) can be computed without re-running, but changing diffusion/drift coefficients requires re-running
rationale: Read Dunzlaff2015 full text. Section 2 gives the SDE recasting and Euler-Maruyama; Section 2.2 lists the advantages (unconditional stability vs finite-difference, no grid, no matrix inversion vs ADI, boundary-independent transition probability); Fig.1/text justify time-backward efficiency (forward wastes particles); Section 4 + Fig.10 give the speedup numbers (11.8/32.5 no fast-math, 26/59.3 with fast-math; abstract says 10-60x). All nuggets verbatim from this single paper; it is the only slice paper deeply covering the SDE-on-GPU method.

intent: What is the evidence that nearby pulsars (rather than dark matter) are the dominant source of the cosmic-ray positron excess seen by PAMELA and AMS-02? Specifically, how do the HAWC (and Milagro) gamma-ray observations of Geminga and B0656+14 feed into that argument?
nuggets: PAMELA and AMS-02 measured an excess of high-energy (~0.01-1 TeV) cosmic-ray positrons over the standard secondary-production prediction; candidate sources include nearby young pulsars and annihilating dark matter

Geminga and B0656+14 are nearby (~250-280 pc), young (~370,000 and ~110,000 yr) pulsars; HAWC and Milagro detect extended (~2 degree) TeV gamma-ray emission from them, produced by inverse-Compton scattering of very-high-energy leptons

The ~2 degree angular extension implies a diffusion coefficient ~10^3 times smaller than the typical ISM value (D ~ 10^27 cm^2/s, near Bohm diffusion), i.e. very-high-energy (>~10 TeV) leptons are trapped within a few parsecs

Sub-TeV positrons can still escape (via convective winds of several hundred km/s or energy-independent diffusion); the HAWC spectral slope (-2.23 at 7 TeV for Geminga) favors a convection-dominated transport scenario

When normalization and spectrum are fixed to the HAWC/Milagro gamma-ray data, Geminga and B0656+14 invariably produce a positron flux similar in spectrum and magnitude to the observed positron fraction, supporting pulsars as the dominant source
The model predicts a distinctive positron-fraction feature near 400-500 GeV from energy losses over Geminga's ~370,000 yr age (E = 1/(b t) ~ 476 GeV)
rationale: Read Hooper2017 full text. Intro confirms the PAMELA/AMS-02 excess and pulsar-vs-dark-matter framing and the Geminga/B0656+14 ages and distances; Section 2 derives the small diffusion coefficient (~10^27 cm^2/s, Bohm-like, factor ~10^3 below ISM) from the ~2 degree extension, the convection scenario favored by HAWC's -2.23 slope, and the trapping of >10 TeV leptons; Section 3 + Fig.5 show the resulting positron fraction matching AMS-02; the 400-500 GeV / 476 GeV feature is stated explicitly. Single-paper, fully self-contained.

intent: Explain the core methodology of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving PDE problems: how is the loss function constructed so the network respects the governing equations, what role does automatic differentiation play, and how does the same machinery let you tackle inverse / ill-posed problems where boundary conditions or parameters are unknown?
nuggets: A fully-connected neural network approximates the PDE solution u(x,t), taking the space-time coordinates as inputs

The composite loss penalizes the PDE residual at randomly sampled collocation/residual points, plus boundary-condition and initial-condition mismatch terms (and an optional data-mismatch term when measurements are available inside the domain)

Automatic differentiation (via the deep-learning framework's chain rule) evaluates the spatial/temporal derivatives in the differential operator exactly, without discretization error and without a mesh

Because data and physics are blended in one loss, PINNs can solve ill-posed inverse problems that conventional CFD cannot (e.g. unknown thermal boundary conditions inferred from a few sparse sensor measurements, or inferring a moving interface and unknown material conductivities in a Stefan problem)

Unknown PDE parameters/coefficients are made trainable and recovered jointly with the solution by minimizing the same loss (in Chen2020, an l0/sparse-regression term plus automatic differentiation is added to discover the closed-form governing PDE from scarce, noisy data)
rationale: Read Cai2021 (firecrawl render of publisher page, but full content): Section 2 gives the network u(x,t), the composite loss L = Lr + Lb + L0 (+ Ldata), automatic differentiation to compute the differential operators, and Sections 3-4 give the inverse/ill-posed cases (unknown thermal BCs from sparse thermocouples; Stefan-problem interface + conductivity inference). Chen2020 confirms DNN solution approximation, data loss + residual physics loss on collocation points, graph-based automatic differentiation for derivatives, and trainable PDE coefficients with l0 sparse regression for equation discovery (originally grep-verified, since content-confirmed against full text — caveat lifted, drill 2026-06-02d). Both directly answer the loss/autodiff/inverse mechanism. Chen2021 (PINN/PRNN for reduced-order modeling), Chiu2021 (coupled AD-ND can-PINN), and Dong2020 (ELM/domain decomposition, explicitly contrasted against PINN) are PINN-adjacent context but answer different specific questions, so they are context not gold.

intent: I keep struggling to get a physics-informed neural network to actually converge to an accurate PDE solution — the loss plateaus and the answer stays wrong. What is the underlying reason PINNs are so hard to train, and what optimizer setup actually helps?
nuggets: The PINN loss landscape is ill-conditioned, with a very large condition number (largest-to-smallest Hessian eigenvalue ratio), which makes first-order optimizers like Adam converge slowly

The ill-conditioning originates specifically in the PDE residual loss term, because it contains the differential operator; an ill-conditioned differential operator induces ill-conditioning in the loss
A PINN only resembles the true PDE solution when the loss is driven to near-zero, so high-accuracy optimization is required rather than just 'low' loss

Combining Adam followed by L-BFGS (Adam+L-BFGS) is superior to either alone: Adam first avoids saddle points, then L-BFGS (a quasi-Newton method) reduces the condition number for faster local convergence
Adam+L-BFGS is still typically under-optimized; a second-order optimizer NysNewton-CG (NNCG) run afterward further reduces the loss and the relative error
rationale: Read Rathore2024 full text (lines 1-383). The abstract + Sections 4-8 explicitly state: PINN loss is ill-conditioned due to differential operators in the residual term (Sec 5, Contributions); quasi-Newton methods improve conditioning by 1000x (Sec 5.3); good solutions require near-zero loss (Sec 4); Adam+L-BFGS is superior across network sizes (Sec 6, Table 1); NNCG further improves results (Sec 7, Table 2); theory connects ill-conditioned operator to ill-conditioned loss (Theorem 8.4). Every nugget is verbatim-supported. Ryck2021 (error/approximation bounds for Kolmogorov PDEs) and Tucny2025 (weight randomness/signal propagation) and Shukla2021 (domain-decomposition parallelism) touch PINN training but do NOT address the loss-landscape/optimizer-difficulty question that is the intent; topical proximity only. Single genuinely-answering paper -> thin.

intent: Walk me through the experimental evidence for the high-energy cosmic-ray positron excess and why it points to either dark matter or nearby pulsars rather than ordinary secondary production. I care about what the space-based magnetic spectrometer experiments actually measured.
nuggets: The positron fraction rises with energy above ~10 GeV, which contradicts standard secondary-production models where the positron fraction should fall smoothly as energy increases (PAMELA, 1.5-100 GeV)
The rising/excess positron component cannot be explained by secondary positrons produced in collisions of cosmic-ray nuclei with interstellar gas, so a primary source is required
The two leading interpretations of the excess are annihilation (or decay) of dark-matter particles in the galactic halo, or production in nearby astrophysical sources such as pulsars
AMS measured the positron flux to ~1 TeV and found it is well described by a low-energy secondary 'diffuse' term plus a high-energy 'source' term with a finite energy cutoff
The AMS source-term cutoff energy is ~810 GeV (Es = 810 +310/-180 GeV), excluded at >4 sigma, and the positron flux shows a sharp drop-off above ~284 GeV
rationale: Read both full texts. Adriani2009 (PAMELA) states the positron fraction increases significantly above 10 GeV (p.7-9), contradicts secondary production, and lists dark-matter halo annihilation and nearby pulsars as candidate primary sources (abstract, p.3, Conclusions). Aguilar2021 (AMS) gives the source+diffuse term decomposition, the 810 +310/-180 GeV cutoff at >4sigma, and the ~284 GeV drop-off (abstract, Sec 1, Eq.2 fit), and explicitly says positrons predominantly originate from dark-matter collisions or new astrophysical sources. Two papers each directly answer different facets -> strong. Aguilar2019 (AMS electrons) is context: it shows electrons differ from positrons but is about the electron excess, not the positron-excess interpretation. Torre2012 is context: it explicitly studies only the <=10 GeV solar-modulation regime and states it does NOT discuss the >10 GeV excess. Abdollahi2017 measures the total e+e- spectrum (break at ~50 GeV), not the positron fraction excess, so off.

intent: When Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause in late 2018, what did the cosmic-ray instrument see, and how did that crossing differ from what Voyager 1 saw? I'm especially interested in any boundary-layer structure just outside the heliopause.
nuggets: On 5 November 2018 (day 309) Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause at 119 au, marked by a sharp simultaneous decrease in low-energy heliospheric/anomalous-cosmic-ray ions and increase in galactic cosmic rays
Unlike Voyager 1, which encountered precursor interstellar flux tubes invading the heliosheath before its crossing, Voyager 2 observed no such precursors before crossing

Just beyond the heliopause Voyager 2 found a cosmic-ray boundary layer where galactic cosmic-ray intensity was only ~90% of the value further out, i.e. GCRs are still modulated in a thin layer outside the heliopause

In that boundary layer low-energy (~0.5-35 MeV) particles streamed outward along the interstellar magnetic field for ~66 days, consistent with field lines connected back to the flank of the heliopause

The mass- and pitch-angle-dependent persistence of anomalous cosmic rays seen at Voyager 1 was NOT observed at Voyager 2, implying different magnetic-field-gradient / diffusion-coefficient conditions at the two crossings
rationale: Read Stone2019 full text. Abstract + Results/Discussion state: crossing at 119 au on 5 Nov 2018 with sharp ion-decrease/GCR-increase (abstract, p.2 day 309); no precursor flux tubes vs Voyager 1's two invading flux tubes (abstract, p.2, Discussion); a boundary layer where GCRs are at ~90% (abstract, p.2 '~90%', Summary); outward streaming of 0.5-35 MeV protons for ~66 d along field connected to the flank (Discussion); ACR mass/pitch-angle persistence seen at V1 but not V2 (Fig.6, Discussion). All five nuggets verbatim-supported. Single paper in my slice covers this -> thin.

intent: Is it actually possible to measure the cosmic-ray electron spectrum up into the TeV range from the ground rather than with balloons or satellites, and what did such a measurement find about the spectral shape at the highest energies?
nuggets: H.E.S.S., an array of ground-based imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes, measured the cosmic-ray electron spectrum at very-high (TeV) energies — the first measurement of this type
The large collection area of ground-based Cherenkov telescopes lets them reach energies beyond what declining-flux direct (balloon/satellite) instruments can access
The measured electron spectrum shows a substantial steepening (softening) above ~600 GeV compared to the lower-energy spectrum
Electron-induced air showers are separated from the dominant hadronic (proton) background using shower shape, and from gamma-rays using the depth of shower maximum
The steep spectrum / energy losses imply the sources of these TeV electrons must be relatively local (within ~1 kpc)
rationale: Read Aharonian2008 (OCR heavily corrupted but key claims legible) + relied on the clean abstract. Abstract states ground-based H.E.S.S. IACT measurement of CR electrons >600 GeV, first of its type, large collection area advantage over balloon/satellite, and substantial steepening above 600 GeV. Body confirms: hadronic background separation via shower parameter zeta and electron/gamma separation via Xmax (p.2-3); local-source (<~1 kpc) implication (p.4 'existence of ... electrons of a local Galaxy (within ~1 kpc)'). I deliberately kept nuggets to robustly-attested qualitative facts and avoided the OCR-mangled numeric values (index ~3.0, cutoff ~2 TeV) to keep gold safe. Aguilar2019 (AMS) and Abdollahi2017 (Fermi) also measure electron spectra but are space-based and do not answer the 'from the ground' intent -> context. Single ground-based paper -> thin.

intent: I'm trying to understand the long-standing tension between drift-based and perpendicular-diffusion-based pictures of how galactic cosmic rays are modulated in the heliosphere. Specifically: why do conventional gradient/curvature-drift models predict that cosmic-ray behaviour should flip between the A>0 and A<0 solar magnetic polarity cycles, and why do Ulysses observations (the small latitudinal gradients, and the latitude dependence of recurrent cosmic-ray decreases) seem to contradict those drift predictions? What role does enhanced/anisotropic perpendicular diffusion play in resolving this?
nuggets: Cosmic-ray transport in the heliosphere is governed by the Parker transport equation, whose terms include convection, gradient/curvature drift (the antisymmetric tensor element K_A), diffusion (parallel K_parallel and perpendicular K_perp), and adiabatic energy changes.

Conventional drift models predict opposite behaviour in the A>0 vs A<0 magnetic polarity epochs because positive particles drift inward over the poles then out along the heliospheric current sheet in A>0, and the reverse in A<0; e.g. drift models predict a large positive latitudinal gradient for protons in A>0, and predict recurrent-decrease amplitudes should be larger in A<0 than A>0.

Ulysses observed only small latitudinal gradients (and, in Dunzlaff, recurrent-decrease latitude behaviour) that contradict the drift-model predictions — the opposite of what drift theory predicts for the two cycles.

Enhancing perpendicular diffusion in the polar direction (anisotropic K_perp, with K_perp_theta > K_perp_r) reduces the latitude dependence of intensities and reconciles drift models with the small latitudinal gradients; perpendicular diffusion dominates electron modulation below ~100 MeV.

Dunzlaff concludes drift effects play only a minor role and instead invokes latitudinal perpendicular diffusion, made efficient by a large stable coronal-hole structure in cycle 22 but not in cycle 23, to explain why the recurrent-decrease periodicity persisted to high latitudes in cycle 22 but vanished in cycle 23.

Both works treat cosmic-ray modulation as a competition/play-off between drift and perpendicular diffusion that varies with position, energy, and the tilt angle of the wavy heliospheric current sheet.
rationale: Read full text of both. Ferreira2000 explicitly states the Parker transport equation (Eq.1) with drift (K_A) and perpendicular diffusion terms, that A>0 drift models predict large positive latitudinal proton gradients, that enhanced K_perp_theta is needed to match the small Ulysses latitudinal gradients, and that perpendicular diffusion dominates below ~100 MeV (Sec.3, Conclusions pts 1-3). Dunzlaff2008 explicitly states drift models predict opposite A>0/A<0 recurrent-decrease behaviour and larger amplitudes in A<0, that Ulysses observations contradict this, and concludes drift is minor while latitudinal perpendicular diffusion in a large stable coronal hole explains cycle 22 vs 23 (Sec.4-6). Both independently and fully address the drift-vs-perp-diffusion tension across polarity cycles.

intent: In solar-wind MHD turbulence there's a well-known puzzle: the magnetic-field power spectrum is usually observed to follow a Kolmogorov k^-5/3 slope, even though the turbulence is Alfvenic and the Iroshnikov-Kraichnan theory would predict a k^-3/2 slope. How does the presence of current sheets in the solar wind explain the emergence of the Kolmogorov scaling, and how was this demonstrated with a cell model of the solar wind?
nuggets: The puzzle: solar-wind MHD turbulence is Alfvenic and Iroshnikov-Kraichnan (IK) theory predicts a k^-3/2 spectrum, yet observations frequently show a Kolmogorov (K41) k^-5/3 slope.
The proposed cause is the presence of current sheets — sharp 2D structures where the magnetic-field direction changes abruptly — which are common in the solar wind.
The cell model represents the solar wind as many randomly-sized cells separated by current sheets, with IK-like (prescribed exponent -3/2) slab turbulence inside each individual cell.

When an imaginary spacecraft trajectory crosses many current sheets (cell boundaries), the measured power spectrum softens/steepens to a Kolmogorov-like k^-5/3 slope even though each cell is locally IK-like.

The result holds across trajectory angles to the background field (fitted indices near -1.66 to -1.72 for theta = 0,15,45,75 deg), confirming that current sheets alter the observed solar-wind MHD turbulence power spectrum.
rationale: Read full text of Li2012. Abstract + Sec.1-4 state exactly: IK predicts k^-3/2, observations show Kolmogorov k^-5/3 (the puzzle), current sheets are the proposed cause, the cell model prescribes IK-like (nu=-1.5) slab turbulence per cell, and crossing many current sheets yields spectra consistent with -5/3 (fitted indices -1.72,-1.67,-1.66,-1.68 in the conclusion). Single isolated topic in my slice (no other read slice paper covers solar-wind turbulence spectral slope) -> thin coverage.

intent: I want the conceptual through-line of how neural networks are used to solve ODEs and PDEs. Start from the early trial-solution approach where the network is embedded in a closed-form trial function, and connect it to the modern physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework. In particular, how does each approach handle the boundary/initial conditions, what is minimized, and what role does automatic differentiation play? Contrast the 'satisfy the boundary conditions by construction' strategy with the 'soft-penalty' strategy.
nuggets: The early approach (Lagaris) writes the trial solution as two terms: a fixed term A(x) that satisfies the initial/boundary conditions exactly by construction (no adjustable parameters) plus a second term containing a feedforward neural network that is constructed so as not to disturb the BCs.

Because the BCs are satisfied by construction, the original constrained optimization is reduced to an unconstrained minimization of the differential-equation residual at collocation points (the network is trained so the ODE/PDE residual goes to zero).

The Lagaris method yields a differentiable closed-form analytic solution with strong interpolation/generalization, and was shown to outperform the finite-element method at non-training (test/interpolation) points.

The modern PINN framework instead enforces the physics as a soft penalty: the loss is a weighted sum of a data term (initial/boundary/measurement mismatch) and a PDE-residual term evaluated at interior collocation points, so the PDE is only approximately satisfied.
PINNs use automatic differentiation to compute the derivatives of the network output needed to form the PDE residual inside the loss function.

Karniadakis frames physics-informed learning via observational, inductive, and learning biases; the soft-penalty PDE-residual-in-loss is the 'learning bias' route, while building BCs/symmetries into the architecture (the Lagaris-style hard constraint) is an 'inductive bias'.
PINNs are especially effective for ill-posed and inverse problems and are mesh-free, whereas for well-posed forward problems classical grid-based solvers can still outperform them.
rationale: Read full text of Lagaris1997 (trial solution = A(x) satisfying BCs by construction + x*N term; constrained->unconstrained min of residual at collocation points; closed-form differentiable; beats FEM at test points -> Sec.2,4.3,5) and ~half of Karniadakis2021 incl. Box 2 (observational/inductive/learning biases) and Box 3 (the PINN soft-penalty loss = w_data*L_data + w_PDE*L_PDE via automatic differentiation), plus 'architectures can be modified to satisfy exactly the required initial/Dirichlet/Neumann conditions' (inductive bias = the Lagaris strategy) and 'PINNs effective for ill-posed/inverse, mesh-free; classical solvers win on well-posed forward'. The contrast (hard-BC-by-construction vs soft-penalty + autodiff) is verbatim supported by both.

intent: I'm interested in using physics-informed neural networks for phase-change / boiling problems, and specifically in the transfer-learning angle: can a PINN trained on the growth of vapour bubbles in one or two superheated working fluids then predict the bubble growth for a completely different working fluid for which you have no observational/CFD data? How well does that work and what makes the bubble-growth case hard?
nuggets: A PINN was developed for heat-and-mass-transfer vapour-bubble growth in a superheated liquid, validated on the classical Scriven bubble benchmark, and tested with three working fluids: water, R-134a, and FC-72.
Forward training used about 50% of the available CFD data for water and R-134a, and the PINN accurately inferred the velocity fields, especially near the bubble interface.

Transfer learning was then used to predict the FC-72 vapour-bubble evolution WITHOUT supplying any observational/CFD data for FC-72 — the network relied on resolving the governing PDEs plus knowledge transferred from the forward cases.

The transfer-learning prediction for the unseen FC-72 bubble achieved a peak error within ~1.3% of the (unobserved) CFD reference; water and R-134a forward cases had peak-error reductions of ~0.87% and ~3.42%.

The hard part is that this is a surface-tension-dominated phase-change problem with a sharp moving liquid-vapour interface, requiring multiple coupled PDEs (mass, momentum/Navier-Stokes with a Weber-number surface-tension term, energy) to be satisfied simultaneously.
rationale: Read abstract + Sec.1-2 of Jalili2024. Abstract states verbatim: three fluids water/R-134a/FC-72, trained on 50% CFD data, peak-error reductions 0.87% (water) and 3.42% (R-134a), FC-72 predicted via transfer learning with NO observational data to within 1.3% peak error, Scriven benchmark, surface-tension-dominated phase change. Sec.2.1 lists the 6 coupled PDEs incl. Navier-Stokes with We surface-tension term and energy equation. Single paper on this specific application in my slice -> thin coverage.

intent: I'm reading up on how solar energetic particle spectra are reconstructed from the neutron-monitor network during ground-level enhancements. For the October 2003 Halloween GLE #65 and GLE #66 events, how did the analysis derive the SEP rigidity spectra and pitch-angle distributions, what functional forms fit best, and what made GLE #66 specifically harder to analyze than GLE #65?
nuggets: Spectra and anisotropy were derived by modeling the global neutron-monitor network response (computing each station's cutoff rigidity and asymptotic directions, then least-squares/optimization unfolding of the inverse problem) over the 1-20 GV rigidity range, at 5-minute time resolution (the NM network being sensitive to primary SEPs above ~300-433 MeV/n).
The SEP rigidity spectrum was best fit by a modified power-law in rigidity (with a steepening term delta-gamma), while the pitch-angle distribution was best fit by a single Gaussian.
During the event the spectra evolved from moderately hard during the initial/main phase to softer (pure power law) later, and the angular distribution gradually broadened over the event.
GLE #66 (29 Oct 2003) occurred during a major geomagnetic storm with planetary Kp ~ 9, which complicated modeling particle propagation in the disturbed magnetosphere.
GLE #66 also occurred during a deep Forbush decrease, whose recovery had to be accounted for in the detrended GCR baseline, interfering with the SEP count-rate increase.

Because of the disturbed magnetosphere, GLE #66 required a more elaborate field model (IGRF internal + Tsyganenko 01 external, via the OTSO tool) whereas the quieter GLE #65 (Kp ~ 4) used IGRF + Tsyganenko 89.
rationale: Read Mishev2024 in full (text_path). The 1-20 GV analysis range is stated VERBATIM ('in the analysis we used the 1-20 GV rigidity range, as described in Section 2'; P_max=20 GV in Eq. 2); the NM network sensitivity floor is ~300 MeV/n (high-mountain polar) / 433 MeV/n (sea-level). Earlier nugget #1 wrote '~0.3-20 GeV/n (1-20 GV)' which conflated the NM-sensitivity threshold with the 1-20 GV fitting window; softened (drill 2026-06-02e, tail 5) to the verbatim 1-20 GV range + the ~300-433 MeV/n NM sensitivity noted separately, so the judge has a clean entailment target. The modified power-law rigidity spectrum (Eqs 3-4) and single-Gaussian PAD (Eq 5) and the hard->soft / broadening evolution are in Section 4.2 + Table 2. The GLE #66 complications (Kp~9 major geomagnetic storm, deep Forbush decrease, IGRF+Tsyganenko 01 via OTSO vs Kp~4 / Tsyganenko 89 for GLE #65) are explicit in Sections 3 and 4.1. No other test100 paper reconstructs these specific events' spectra, so single-paper strong coverage is correct.

intent: I want to understand the large-scale structure of the interplanetary (heliospheric) magnetic field as mapped by in-situ spacecraft: how the average field follows the Parker spiral and how its radial fall-off depends on solar-wind speed, how the sector structure is organized into a tilted wavy current sheet and how corotating interaction regions distort it, and how the small-scale turbulent fluctuations of that field are anisotropic relative to the mean field and vary with solar-wind speed.
nuggets: The average interplanetary field follows the Archimedean (Parker) spiral, with the radial component falling as R^-2 and the azimuthal component as ~R^-1; Pioneer 10 data agree once the long-term increase in solar-wind speed is folded in (the azimuthal-times-speed product B_phi*V varies as R^-1).

The sector structure is explained by a current sheet that is approximately flat but tilted near the Sun, which develops a large-scale wavy ('wobbling') structure as the Sun rotates and the plasma is carried outward; two stable Parker-spiral sectors dominate the long-term field.
The latitudinal extent (tilt) of the current-sheet warp decreases toward solar minimum (the warp is smaller at sunspot minimum).

Corotating interaction regions (CIRs), formed where fast solar-wind streams compress the field, can deform and absorb the current sheet, typically through the forward shock, so sector boundaries are often found at the leading edges of CIRs.

Solar-wind magnetic turbulence is anisotropic relative to the mean field: the correlation scale is longest parallel to the mean field in slow and intermediate wind (parallel/perpendicular ratio ~2.5 slow, ~2.15 intermediate) but the ratio drops to ~0.71 in fast wind.
This anisotropy implies quasi-two-dimensional turbulence dominates in slow/intermediate solar wind while slab-type turbulence dominates in fast solar wind.
rationale: All three read in full. Parker1976 (Pioneer 10): R^-2 radial, ~R^-1 azimuthal, B_phi*V ~ R^-1, best-fit R^-1.1, speed correction (Intro + Long-Term Variations sections + Table 1). Thomas1981: flat-but-tilted current sheet developing a wavy structure from solar rotation, two dominant Parker-spiral sectors, tilt decreasing toward minimum, CIRs deforming/absorbing the sheet via the forward shock (Average Current Sheet Structure + Effect of CIRs sections). Weygand2011: correlation-scale anisotropy 2.55/2.15/0.71 for slow/intermediate/fast wind and the 2D-vs-slab interpretation (abstract + Section 3.1-3.2, Table 1). The three jointly cover spiral + current sheet + turbulence; coverage is genuinely strong (3 directly-answering papers).

intent: Voyager 1 found that anomalous cosmic-ray oxygen does not show the simple shock-accelerated spectrum peaking at the solar-wind termination shock; instead the spectrum is highly modulated at the shock and the ACR intensity keeps rising deeper into the heliosheath, away from the supposed source. What acceleration/transport mechanism has been proposed to explain this, and how does the model reproduce the Voyager observations?
nuggets: The model solves the Parker transport equation in 2D including, beyond diffusive shock (Fermi I) acceleration at the termination shock, momentum diffusion (Fermi II / stochastic acceleration) and adiabatic heating occurring within the heliosheath.

Adiabatic heating plus Fermi II re-acceleration cause ACR oxygen intensities to increase away from the termination shock and peak well inside the heliosheath (for energies below ~6-10 MeV/nuc), explaining why intensity rises toward the heliopause instead of peaking at the shock.

Fermi II (momentum diffusion) acceleration is most effective in the outer heliosheath near the heliopause, where the assumed solar-wind speed profile makes the Alfven speed rise sharply (momentum diffusion depends on V_A).

The model uses a latitude-dependent termination-shock compression ratio and PUI injection efficiency (both maximal in the equatorial/nose region and lower toward the poles), giving a region of preferred acceleration near the equatorial termination shock.

With these ingredients the model reproduces the Voyager 1 heliosheath O observations, including both the modulated spectral form at the termination shock and its unfolding (hardening) as the spacecraft moves into the heliosheath.
rationale: Read Strauss2010 in full. Abstract + Section 1 frame the puzzle (highly modulated ACR spectra, intensities increasing into the heliosheath, classical paradigm violated at V1/V2). Section 2 (Eq 1) shows Parker transport with momentum-diffusion term and the latitude-dependent s(theta), I(theta) (Eqs 5-6). Section 4.2 + Section 5 conclusions state Fermi II + adiabatic heating cause intensities to increase into the heliosheath, most effective in outer heliosheath near HP where V_A rises, and that the model reproduces V1 spectra/radial profiles (Figs 6-7). Only Strauss2010 in my slice models ACR-O re-acceleration; note that the broader corpus has heliosheath/termination-shock GCR papers (e.g. Kolesnik2012) and Voyager interstellar measurements (Stone2019), but those address GCR modulation / interstellar flux, not the ACR-oxygen re-acceleration mechanism, so single-paper thin coverage is correct.

intent: I'm writing the discussion section of a paper on the cosmic-ray positron excess and I need to lay out, line of evidence by line of evidence, whether the excess actually requires dark-matter annihilation or whether nearby pulsars plus solar-modulation systematics can absorb it. Specifically: what spectral features did PAMELA and AMS-02 actually measure, what does the HAWC pulsar evidence say, what do the AMS-02 antiprotons do to the heavy-DM hypothesis, and how much of the low-energy structure is really just charge-sign-dependent solar modulation rather than a primary source? Where do these explanations genuinely conflict?
nuggets: PAMELA (Adriani2009) discovered that the positron fraction RISES with energy above ~10 GeV (1.5-100 GeV range), contradicting the smooth fall predicted by pure secondary production (Moskalenko & Strong), and explicitly framed the rise as requiring either dark-matter annihilation or nearby pulsars, while noting none of the published models fit the data well.

AMS-02 (Aguilar2021) sharpened the positron excess into a quantitative spectral signature: an onset at 25.2 +/- 1.8 GeV, a maximum near ~290 GeV, and a finite source-term exponential cutoff energy E_s = 810 (+310/-180) GeV established at more than 4 sigma (4.07 sigma) significance.

Hooper2017 argues that HAWC (plus Milagro) TeV gamma-ray observations of Geminga and B0656+14 show these nearby pulsars inject enough high-energy e+e- that pulsars INVARIABLY produce a positron flux similar in spectrum and magnitude to the PAMELA/AMS-02 excess, making them the likely dominant source.

Cuoco2017 shows that the AMS-02 ANTIPROTON spectrum is fit well by purely secondary antiprotons (no primary/DM component required) and sets robust limits that strongly disfavor thermal heavy DM (e.g. the ~2.8 TeV thermal wino) - so a DM explanation of the positron excess must avoid overproducing antiprotons.

The DM-vs-pulsar debate hinges on whether the same source must show up in antiprotons: leptophilic/pulsar explanations evade the antiproton constraint, whereas generic WIMP annihilation into quarks/gauge bosons is squeezed by Cuoco2017's antiproton limits, a tension the positron data alone (Aguilar2021, Adriani2009) cannot resolve.

Potgieter2021 demonstrates that a large part of the LOW-energy positron behavior is charge-sign-dependent solar (drift) modulation tied to the 22-year heliospheric polarity cycle - significant below a few GeV - and that the simple force-field approximation used by AMS-02 is inadequate for antimatter, meaning sub-GeV structure is a modulation systematic rather than a primary-source signal.

The lines of evidence conflict on locality and on antiprotons: PAMELA/AMS-02 establish the excess but cannot identify the source; Hooper2017 attributes it to nearby pulsars; Cuoco2017 uses antiprotons to disfavor heavy DM; and Potgieter2021 warns that the low-energy end is contaminated by modulation systematics - so the excess does NOT uniquely require dark matter.
rationale: Read in full: Adriani2009, Aguilar2021, Hooper2017, Potgieter2021; read full conclusion + methods/results of Cuoco2017. Nugget 1 = Adriani2009 abstract, 'HIGH ENERGY ANOMALY' section and conclusions, Table I. Nugget 2 = Aguilar2021 abstract and section 1 (E_s=810 GeV excluded at 4.07 sigma). Nugget 3 = Hooper2017 abstract, introduction, conclusions. Nugget 4 = Cuoco2017 section 2.1 (secondary antiprotons fit well, not required) and section 4 conclusion (strongly disfavor thermal wino regardless of DM profile). Nugget 5 synthesizes Cuoco2017's quark/gauge-boson limits against positron-only inference of Aguilar2021/Adriani2009. Nugget 6 = Potgieter2021 abstract, section 1 (force-field inadequate, misleading), section 9; charge-sign point corroborated in Adriani2009. Nugget 7 = synthesis across the four directly-answering papers plus modulation caveat. Off: Abdollahi2017 and Aguilar2019 are about the electron side / combined spectrum, off-target for the positron-excess origin debate.

intent: I'm trying to understand the leptonic spectral asymmetry that the dark-matter-vs-pulsar interpretations have to explain. Why do AMS-02 see a sharp cutoff in the positron flux but none in the electron flux, and how does that square with the Fermi-LAT combined electron-plus-positron spectrum and the original PAMELA positron-fraction rise? I specifically want the measured numbers - onset energies, cutoff energies and their significances, spectral indices - across the experiments, and I want to know what this positron/electron asymmetry implies for whether a single dark-matter source can produce equal electrons and positrons or whether separate (e.g. pulsar) sources are required.
nuggets: AMS-02 (Aguilar2021) measure a positron flux with a finite exponential source-term cutoff at E_s = 810 (+310/-180) GeV (>4 sigma), whereas AMS-02 (Aguilar2019) find the ELECTRON flux has NO exponential cutoff below 1.9 TeV at the 5 sigma level - a direct positron/electron asymmetry.

The positron excess onset (25.2 +/- 1.8 GeV, Aguilar2021) and the electron excess onset (42.1 +5.4/-5.2 GeV, Aguilar2019) occur at different energies and the AMS Collaboration explicitly states the electron excess is of a DIFFERENT NATURE from the positron excess, evidence that most high-energy electrons come from different sources than high-energy positrons.

Aguilar2019 tested whether a dark-matter-like source term identical to the positron source term exists in the electrons and found the electron data are consistent BOTH with the presence and with the absence of such a term - so the electron spectrum alone cannot confirm or exclude a common DM source.

Fermi-LAT (Abdollahi2017) measured the combined electron+positron spectrum from 7 GeV to 2 TeV, fit it as a broken power law with a break near 50 GeV and an index of 3.07 +/- 0.02 above the break, and EXCLUDED an exponential cutoff below 1.8 TeV at 95% CL - consistent with the no-cutoff electron behavior but in tension with the 810 GeV positron cutoff being a feature of the total lepton flux.

PAMELA (Adriani2009) originally established the anomaly as a RISING positron FRACTION above ~10 GeV (a ratio), which the later AMS-02 flux measurements (Aguilar2021/Aguilar2019) resolved into separately-shaped positron and electron FLUXES - clarifying that the rising fraction is driven by the distinct positron component.

Hooper2017's pulsar model naturally predicts a positron spectrum with an energy-loss feature around 400-500 GeV (e.g. ~476 GeV for Geminga's ~370,000-year age) and a cutoff, providing an astrophysical explanation for the positron flux drop-off without invoking an electron cutoff at the same energy - matching the observed positron/electron asymmetry.

The combined picture forces a choice: a generic DM source producing equal e+ and e- is hard to reconcile with the asymmetry (cutoff in positrons but not electrons), favoring source classes like pulsars that inject e+e- with a positron-side spectral feature, while DM is not excluded because the electron data are agnostic (Aguilar2019).
rationale: Read in full: Aguilar2021, Aguilar2019, Adriani2009, Hooper2017; read Abdollahi2017 results in full. Nugget 1 = Aguilar2021 (positron cutoff 810 GeV >4 sigma) and Aguilar2019 (electron no cutoff below 1.9 TeV at 5 sigma). Nugget 2 = Aguilar2019 abstract (onset 42.1 GeV, 'different nature') and Aguilar2021 (positron onset 25.2 GeV). Nugget 3 = Aguilar2019 (electron data consistent both with and without an identical source term). Nugget 4 = Abdollahi2017 abstract and section VII (break ~50 GeV, index 3.07, exclude cutoff below 1.8 TeV 95% CL). Nugget 5 = Adriani2009 positron-fraction sections contrasted with AMS flux measurements (why Adriani2009 is context). Nugget 6 = Hooper2017 (feature 400-500 GeV, 476 GeV for Geminga 370 kyr). Nugget 7 = synthesis tying Aguilar2019's agnosticism to Hooper2017's positron feature and the measured asymmetry. Off: Cuoco2017 (antiprotons) and Potgieter2021 (modulation) are other observables, mis-retrievals for the e+/e- spectral-shape question. All numbers verbatim from read text.

intent: I'm trying to adjudicate the central debate over the sub-TeV cosmic-ray proton/nuclei spectral hardening: is the ~200-400 GV break an intrinsic source/injection effect, a Galactic propagation (diffusion-coefficient) effect, or partly an artifact of stitching together experiments whose absolute energy scales disagree? I want each camp's actual evidence laid side by side - the specific break rigidities different experiments report, the argument that ties the break to propagation rather than injection, and the explicit treatment of inter-experiment energy-scale offsets - so I can see which interpretation each paper's data actually supports.
nuggets: PAMELA (Adriani2011) directly observes a hardening in the proton spectrum at a break rigidity of 232 (+35/-30) GV, where the spectral index changes from ~2.85 (80-232 GV) to ~2.67 (>232 GV), with helium hardening at a similar rigidity (~243 GV).

AMS-02 places the proton hardening at a higher rigidity (~336 GV) than PAMELA's ~232 GV, and Lipari2019's global fit across PAMELA/AMS-02/calorimeters centers the hardening near ~650 GeV with a larger spectral-index step than the magnetic spectrometers alone indicate.

Schroer2021 argues the break at ~300 GV must be a propagation effect - a break in the Galactic diffusion coefficient (Rb ~290-300 GV in their D(R)) - NOT an injection/source effect, because the same break appears in secondary-to-primary ratios, which would not happen if the feature originated at the accelerators.

Adriani2011 (PAMELA) frames the hardening instead as a possible source effect, comparing to multi-source models (e.g. Zatsepin-Sokolskaya with novae/superbubble sources) and stating the data challenge the standard single-population SNR-acceleration-plus-diffusive-propagation paradigm (GALPROP does not reproduce the data).

The apparent disagreement in break rigidity and spectral indices between experiments is in large part a cross-calibration problem: Dembinski2017 shows each experiment's energy scale carries a ~10-20% systematic uncertainty that, for a spectral index ~2.7, produces ~18% apparent flux shifts, and derives explicit energy-scale offset/adjustment factors from a global fit.

Lipari2019 attributes the systematically softer slope above the break seen by AMS-02 (alpha2 ~2.72) versus the calorimeters (alpha2 ~2.44-2.62) to AMS-02's limited maximum rigidity (~1.2-1.8 TV) not capturing the full development of the hardening - i.e. a measurement-range/energy-scale effect, not a real spectral disagreement.

Lipari2019 explicitly enumerates that post-PAMELA models attribute the hardening to EITHER acceleration (two accelerator classes / two acceleration regimes) OR propagation (rigidity-dependent diffusion changing regime), leaving the source-vs-propagation question open.
rationale: Read in full: Adriani2011, Lipari2019, Schroer2021, Dembinski2017; Maurin2019 read in full but is the USINE propagation-code tool paper, does not adjudicate the break, so off. Nugget 1 = Adriani2011 (proton hardening 232 GV, 2.85->2.67; helium 243 GV). Nugget 2 = Lipari2019 Table 1 (AMS-02 break ~336 GV vs PAMELA 232 GV; combined Eb ~650 GeV). Nugget 3 = Schroer2021 Intro/section II (break ~300 GV must be transport not injection; appears in secondary/primary; Rb ~290-300 GV). Nugget 4 = Adriani2011 (Zatsepin-Sokolskaya multi-source, challenge paradigm, GALPROP fails). Nugget 5 = Dembinski2017 section 2 (10% offset -> 18% flux for alpha=2.7; 10-20% energy-scale uncertainty; GSF offsets). Nugget 6 = Lipari2019 (AMS-02 alpha2 ~2.716 vs calorimeters 2.44-2.62, attributed to max rigidity). Nugget 7 = Lipari2019 section 4 (acceleration-vs-propagation enumeration). Discrimination: source-claim, propagation-claim, energy-scale-artifact, and cross-experiment framing are in four different papers.

intent: I want to test how 'universal' the cosmic-ray spectral features really are across species and across the energy decades, and where the universality breaks down. Specifically: do protons, helium, and heavier nuclei share a common rigidity-dependent hardening/softening shape, or do they require different source spectra? Where does a single self-consistent transport model succeed, and what are the documented anomalies (the proton/helium index difference, the iron low-rigidity anomaly, the second softening, and the PeV-region experimental disagreements) that no single picture cleanly explains?
nuggets: PAMELA (Adriani2011) finds proton and helium have DIFFERENT spectral shapes/indices - the proton index (~2.82, 30-1000 GV) is steeper than helium (~2.73), a robust difference of Delta-gamma = gamma_p - gamma_He ~= 0.101 - already breaking the assumption of a single universal source spectrum for all species.

Schroer2021 independently concludes that protons, helium, and heavier nuclei require slightly DIFFERENT injection (source) spectra - H softer by ~0.05, He harder by ~0.02 relative to heavier nuclei - which is at odds with rigidity-only diffusive shock acceleration and corroborates the PAMELA p/He difference.

The hardening (and the higher-energy softening at ~10-20 TeV) appears to have an approximately 'universal' rigidity-dependent shape common to protons, helium and other primary nuclei, per Lipari2019, though the slope values differ between species - a universality that holds for the FEATURE shape even while the underlying source slopes differ.

Schroer2021 documents the iron anomaly: AMS-02 Fe is anomalously hard at R < ~100 GV and its Fe/O ratio is in tension with the standard transport model AND with HEAO/ACE-CRIS/Voyager data, a discrepancy (~30-40% near 1 GeV/n) that the authors cannot resolve and suspect may be experimental.

A single set of Galactic transport parameters (diffusion + advection, with a high-rigidity break in the diffusion coefficient) consistently fits intermediate and heavy nuclei (Ne, Mg, Si, S up to Fe except the iron low-rigidity anomaly) per Schroer2021, supporting the propagation-break interpretation for most species.

Semi-analytical propagation tools like USINE (Maurin2019) are the machinery used to fit this picture - solving the diffusion/advection transport equation for Z=1-30 nuclei with force-field solar modulation - and USINE was used to hint at the high-rigidity break in the diffusion coefficient from AMS-02 B/C data, the same propagation break invoked to explain the hardening.

Dembinski2017's data-driven global spline fit deliberately avoids assuming power-law-plus-cutoff component shapes and instead cross-calibrates experiment energy scales across 10 GeV to 10^11 GeV, showing the all-particle and per-element structure (the ~5 TeV dip, the knee at ~3 PeV) emerges from a world-average once energy scales are reconciled rather than from one source/propagation model.
rationale: Read in full: all five papers. Nugget 1 = Adriani2011 (gamma_p ~2.820, gamma_He ~2.732, Delta-gamma=0.101). Nugget 2 = Schroer2021 section IV.C/Conclusions (three slopes: proton ~0.05 softer, He ~0.02 harder; at odds with DSA). Nugget 3 = Lipari2019 section 4 (universal rigidity-dependent shape across species even if slopes differ). Nugget 4 = Schroer2021 abstract/IV.B (iron hard R<100 GV, Fe/O tension with model and HEAO/ACE-CRIS/Voyager, ~30-40% at 1 GeV/n, possibly experimental). Nugget 5 = Schroer2021 section III-IV (single transport set fits Ne/Mg/Si/S/Fe except iron). Nugget 6 = Maurin2019 (USINE Z=1-30, force-field, hints high-rigidity diffusion break from AMS-02 B/C). Nugget 7 = Dembinski2017 (GSF no power-law assumption; energy-scale cross-calibration; 5 TeV dip, 3 PeV knee emerge from world-average). Maurin2019/Dembinski2017 context (tool + framework) not direct adjudicators of species universality.

intent: I'm building a heliospheric cosmic-ray modulation code and trying to decide whether to solve Parker's transport equation with stochastic differential equations (pseudo-particle/Markov solvers) or with a finite-difference grid scheme like ADI. I want to understand the concrete numerical trade-offs each group reports (stability, parallelism/cost, what part of phase space you get a solution at, dimensionality limits), and crucially whether groups fitting the SAME modern proton/helium spectra (PAMELA, AMS-02) with these different numerics end up recovering consistent diffusion-coefficient behavior and rigidity dependence. Pull from both the SDE-solver methodology papers and the application papers that fit spacecraft data.
nuggets: Parker's equation is traditionally solved by finite-difference schemes such as the Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) method, whereas the SDE/pseudo-particle approach is the increasingly popular alternative (Dunzlaff2015; Corti2018; Song2021).

SDEs are unconditionally (numerically) stable while finite-difference/ADI schemes can become unstable for too-large time steps, and time-dependent 3D ADI is numerically unsuitable/unstable so that one spatial dimension must be sacrificed or the SDE approach adopted (Dunzlaff2015; Corti2018; Song2021).

An SDE/pseudo-particle solver computes the solution only at the phase-space point(s) of interest (a spectrum at Earth) and is embarrassingly parallel with independent trajectories, whereas a finite-difference solver computes f over the whole grid; the time-backward SDE formulation is the efficient choice for spectra at a point (Dunzlaff2015).

Corti2018 uses a 3D steady-state finite-difference (ADI) solver and, because a single model run is slow, fits AMS-02 monthly proton fluxes by generating a multi-million-model parameter grid (~3 million models, ~10 weeks, 4.6 TB) and interpolating, rather than a per-flux least-squares minimization (Corti2018 section 3).

Song2021 solves the SAME class of PAMELA/AMS-02 proton+helium spectra (2006-2017) with a time-dependent 3D SDE solver but searches the drift/diffusion parameter space with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC, Metropolis-Hastings), achieving best-fit normalized chi^2 mostly < 1 (Song2021).

Multiple groups, despite different numerics, agree that the parallel diffusion coefficient magnitude (normalization K_0 and a double-power-law rigidity dependence with K_perp ~= 0.02 K_parallel) is anticorrelated with solar activity and must vary in time to reproduce the spectra (Song2021; Wang2019; Ngobeni2020; Corti2018).

There is a documented partial DISAGREEMENT in the inferred rigidity dependence: Song2021 (SDE+MCMC best-fit) finds the parallel-MFP rigidity slope can be STEEPER at low rigidity than high rigidity during moderate/minimum activity, contrary to the steepening-at-high-rigidity reported by steady-state ADI-style models, and Song2021 explicitly attributes such differences partly to steady-state-vs-time-dependent and ADI-vs-SDE numerics (Song2021 section 4.3).

Wang2019 solves Parker's equation with the SolarProp SDE Monte-Carlo code in 2D time-dependent form, fitting Voyager-1 + PAMELA to derive the LIS, and finds an empirical power-law DC ~ <B_E>^-n with n ~= 2 between the diffusion coefficient and the near-Earth HMF (Wang2019).
rationale: Read in full: Dunzlaff2015, Song2021, Wang2019; Corti2018 and Ngobeni2020 read through methods+results. Zhao2013a: ABSTRACT-ONLY - the on-disk extract is a MISMATCHED paper (DOI 10.1002/jgra.50235, an observation-based heavy-nuclei model that does not solve Parker's equation), so grounded only on the get_paper abstract and used as low-weight context. Nugget 2 = Dunzlaff2015 2.2 (SDE unconditionally stable, FD not), Corti2018 (time-dependence makes ADI unsuitable), Song2021 (time-backward SDE unconditional stability). intent: Across the modulation groups that reproduce the proton-to-helium ratio from PAMELA and AMS-02, I want to know whether the physical conclusion - that the time/rigidity behavior of p/He below a few GV is driven by the mass-to-charge ratio A/Z and by the different proton vs helium local interstellar spectra rather than by species-dependent diffusion - is robust to the numerical solver used (3D steady-state finite-difference ADI vs 3D/2D SDE pseudo-particle, with parameters set by grid-scan vs MCMC vs manual tuning). I also want the shared modeling assumption that the same diffusion/drift coefficients (same mean free paths in rigidity) apply to protons and helium, and where the groups note residual quantitative discrepancies.
nuggets: It is a shared assumption across these models that protons and helium share the SAME diffusion/drift coefficients (the same mean free paths as a function of rigidity), so one parameter set reproduces both species' spectra simultaneously (Ngobeni2020; Corti2018; Song2021).

Corti2018, using a 3D steady-state finite-difference ADI solver, concludes the dependence of the diffusion tensor on the particle mass-to-charge ratio A/Z is the MAIN cause of the time dependence of p/He below ~3 GV (Corti2018 abstract).

Ngobeni2020, using a 3D drift (finite-difference, steady-state) model fitting PAMELA p and He 2006-2009, concludes the p/He differences arise from the combined effect of A/Z and especially the DIFFERENT proton vs helium VLIS slopes, with p/He above ~3-4 GV settling near ~5.5 essentially independent of modulation conditions and thus revealing the VLIS shapes (Ngobeni2020).

Ngobeni2020 explicitly shows all mean free paths and the drift scale are independent of A/Z (A/Z enters only through beta = v/c in the rigidity-to-energy conversion), so there is no fundamental species-difference in modulation at a given rigidity - the p/He time/rigidity structure comes from beta(A/Z) and the VLIS (Ngobeni2020 section 2.1).

Song2021 (3D time-dependent SDE + MCMC) reproduces the long-term time dependence of the AMS-02/PAMELA p/He but finds the simulated ratio systematically LOWER than observed, attributing the residual to underestimation of the proton flux / the assumed proton LIS - a quantitative discrepancy that the steady-state groups also flag as LIS-sensitivity (Song2021 section 4.2).

All four groups specify the modulation boundary at the heliopause/termination shock (Song2021 heliopause 120 au; Corti2018 termination shock 80 au, heliopause 122 au; Ngobeni2020 heliopause 122 au; Wang2019 termination shock 100 au) where the LIS/VLIS is imposed as the boundary condition, and all use a Parker/Smith-Bieber-type HMF with K_perp ~= 0.02 K_parallel.

Wang2019 (2D time-dependent SolarProp SDE) shares modulation parameters across CR species (p, He, B, C) in the same period and derives their LIS by fitting Voyager-1 + PAMELA/BESS/ACE, reinforcing the cross-group view that one diffusion parameterization serves multiple nuclei and that the LIS is the key species-distinguishing input (Wang2019).
